The Six-banded armadillo (Euphractus sexcinctus) exhibits a remarkable basal metabolic rate during its active phase, with respirometry trials conducted at a core body temperature of 33.6 °C [T = 33.6 °C] revealing a maximum oxygen consumption of 1237 milliliters per hour [JOi = 1237 milliliters per hour]. This relatively elevated metabolic rate, measured in captive individuals under thermoneutral conditions, likely reflects the species' active foraging lifestyle and its need to excavate termite mounds and carrion from the semiarid Brazilian Caatinga. In comparison to other armadillo species, the metabolic intensity of this medium-sized xenarthran appears consistent with a diet rich in protein and fat rather than the energetically costly processing of plant matter. The maintenance of such a high metabolic output at the species' typical operating temperature underscores the substantial daily energy requirements faced by this solitary forager in its seasonally dry habitats.

Newborn offspring of the Six-banded armadillo are remarkably precocial, weighing approximately 105 grams [Wwb = approximately 105 grams] at the moment of parturition based on field measurements recorded from captive breeding colonies. This neonatal mass, which generally falls within a reported range of 95 to 115 grams, represents a considerable maternal investment given that adult females can ultimately reach an asymptotic mass of 8200 grams [Wwi = 8200 grams]. The relatively large size of the singleton or twin pups at birth may shorten the vulnerable period of complete dependency on the mother. Maternal expenditure is further underscored by the substantial mass at the conclusion of the suckling stage, with young weanlings scaling up to around 420 grams [Wwx = around 420 grams] by the time they transition fully to solid foods derived from their insectivorous and carnivorous diet.

The reproductive schedule of Euphractus sexcinctus is constrained by a relatively extended gestation period of 28 days [tg = 28 days] measured under stable captive conditions at 33.6 °C [T = 33.6 °C], a comparatively moderate duration among the Dasypodidae. Following parturition, the mother provides intensive lactational support for a distinct interval, with the offspring typically achieving nutritional independence at 68 days after birth [tx = 68 days after birth] under that same thermal regime at a temperature of 33.6 °C [T = 33.6 °C]. This prolonged period of maternal care, during which the dependent pups grow rapidly from their natal mass, likely facilitates the development of robust digging abilities and the complex behavioral repertoire required for independent survival. The interval from birth to weaning is thus a critical phase in the species' life history.

Sexual maturation in the Six-banded armadillo occurs relatively late in the juvenile period, with field and captive data indicating that puberty is attained at approximately 274 days after birth [tp = approximately 274 days after birth] under standard thermal conditions of 33.6 °C [T = 33.6 °C]. This delayed onset of reproductive capability, combined with a modest annual output, suggests that the species follows a relatively slow life-history strategy for a mammal of its body size. Females produce just one litter per year [F_R_i = one litter per year] consisting of two young [N_R_i = two young], a rate that limits the potential for rapid population growth. This combination of delayed maturity, a small two-offspring litter produced annually, and extended maternal investment is consistent with a strategy adapted to environments where juvenile survival may be low due to predation by large carnivores and birds of prey.

Maximum documented longevity for the Six-banded armadillo under seminatural conditions extends to approximately 22.1 years [am = approximately 22.1 years], a value recorded in captive individuals maintained at a consistent environmental temperature of 33.6 °C [T = 33.6 °C]. This impressive lifespan is notable among medium-sized xenarthrans and may be linked to a relatively slow pace of cellular metabolism despite the species' high peak BMR. Older individuals in the wild eventually succumb to natural mortality associated with senescence, including progressive tooth wear that impairs their ability to process carrion and hard-bodied insects. The species' semelparous annual reproductive strategy, with females investing heavily in a single small litter each year over a long adult life, appears to buffer population persistence against the stochastic environmental conditions typical of its harsh savanna and scrubland habitats.
